\section[Iānuārius, Februārius, Mārtius, Aprīlis, Māius, Iūnius, Quīntīlis, Sextīlis, September, Octōber, November, December]{Iānuārius to December — the twelve months, before and after the rename}

\label{lesson:LA-C11-menses}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You'll meet these twelve names again, worn down, in Spanish and French. Latin lets you see something they can't show you directly: \textbf{two of these months used to have completely different names.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{who / what} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Iānuārius} & \textbf{Janus}, the two-faced god of doors and beginnings \\
\textbf{Februārius} & \emph{Februa}, the Roman \textbf{purification} festival \\
\textbf{Mārtius} & \textbf{Mars}, the war-god \\
\textbf{Aprīlis} & perhaps \textbf{aperīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to open\textquotedblright{} (buds opening) \\
\textbf{Māius} & \textbf{Maia}, goddess of growth \\
\textbf{Iūnius} & \textbf{Juno}, queen of the gods \\
\textbf{Quīntīlis} & literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the fifth}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{quīntus}) — \textbf{later renamed Iūlius} \\
\textbf{Sextīlis} & literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the sixth}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{sextus}) — \textbf{later renamed Augustus} \\
\textbf{September} & \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the seventh}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{septem}) \\
\textbf{Octōber} & \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the eighth}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{octō}) \\
\textbf{November} & \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the ninth}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{novem}) \\
\textbf{December} & \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the tenth}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{decem}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
You'll often hear that \textbf{Julius Caesar and Augustus \textquotedblleft{}added\textquotedblright{} two months} to the calendar, which is why September through December no longer match their numbers. That's \textbf{not what happened}. Rome's year, centuries earlier, had already been expanded from ten months to twelve by adding \textbf{Iānuārius} and \textbf{Februārius} at the front — that's the real reason \emph{September} (\textquotedblleft{}seventh\textquotedblright{}) ended up as the \textbf{ninth} month.

\emph{Quīntīlis} (\textquotedblleft{}the fifth\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{Sextīlis} (\textquotedblleft{}the sixth\textquotedblright{}) already existed as ordinary, plainly-numbered months, right alongside \emph{September} through \emph{December}. Long after Julius Caesar's death, the Senate simply \textbf{renamed} \emph{Quīntīlis} to \textbf{Iūlius} in his honor; decades later, Augustus received the same honor, and \emph{Sextīlis} became \textbf{Augustus}. No months were created — two old, numbered ones just got new names, and Latin's fifth and sixth months quietly disappeared from view, hiding inside \emph{julio/juillet} and \emph{agosto/août} in every daughter language.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the twelve — \textquotedblleft{}Iānuārius, Februārius, Mārtius, Aprīlis, Māius, Iūnius, Quīntīlis, Sextīlis, September, Octōber, November, December\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the originals — \textquotedblleft{}Quīntīlis, the fifth\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Sextīlis, the sixth\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the correction — \textquotedblleft{}renamed, not inserted\textquotedblright{}{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What were \emph{Iūlius} and \emph{Augustus} called \textbf{before} they were renamed, and what did those names mean? (\textbf{Quīntīlis} \textquotedblleft{}the fifth\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{Sextīlis} \textquotedblleft{}the sixth.\textquotedblright{}) Did Julius Caesar and Augustus add new months to the calendar? (\textbf{No} — they got two already-existing months \textbf{renamed} after them.) What actually caused \emph{September–December} to fall out of step with their numbers? (\textbf{Adding Iānuārius and Februārius} to the front of the year, centuries earlier.)
\end{tcolorbox}
